text:
More than 100 well-known writers and members of the literary world are to form a splinter chapter of PEN America, the free-expression literary and human rights group, over tensions within the organization over Israel’s war in Gaza and other issues.
Writers including Ta-Nehisi Coates, M Gessen and Jacqueline Woodson are among those who on Monday announced they are forming a new group called PEN Writes US that will be “guided by the PEN Charter’s vision of ‘one humanity, living in peace and equality in one world’”.
The group describes itself as an “aspiring PEN chapter founded by writers, translators, artists, editors, agents, and booksellers” from all over the US. The group says it is supported by PEN International while it aims “to build a new home for writers committed to free expression, and their range of backgrounds, languages, and perspectives is our greatest strength”.
“We seek to join more than 140 PEN Centers worldwide (and the many that have coexisted in the United States) in mobilizing writers at every stage of their career to defend free expression, support writers and artists at risk, and champion reading, translation, and literature,” it added.
PEN America told the Associated Press that it remains focused on “defending free expression as a universal right that must be protected regardless of viewpoint”.
Novelist Maaza Mengiste told the outlet that the new group does not seek to be a rival of PEN America and will probably share common ground about fighting censorship and oppression and encouraging discussions among writers.
Mengiste said that PEN Writes will differ in its structure and in some of its priorities, ideally becoming “a center where sustained and equal advocacy for all writers guides principles, rather than institutional caution”.
The formation of PEN Writes comes as PEN America has faced criticism from numerous writers and activists who say they are unhappy with the latter group’s response to Israel’s war in Gaza. Critics argue that PEN America has been reluctant to criticize Israel or to defend the rights of Palestinian writers with the same force it has advocated for writers elsewhere.
“I think there’s been a feeling for quite a while that PEN’s response to the war in Gaza has been inadequate,” says PEN Writes member Francine Prose, a former president of PEN America, according to the AP.
Fallout from the war in Gaza led PEN America to call off its annual awards show and World Voices festival in 2024 because so many participants dropped out.
Those events resumed. But in June, Dinaw Mengestu resigned as PEN America president after PEN published a report about obstacles and harassment faced by Israeli and Jewish writers since Israel began waging war in Gaza in 2023 in the wake of the 7 October attacks by Hamas that year.
Mengestu, a prize-winning novelist who is now a member of PEN Writes, at the time cited the report’s criticism of cultural boycotts. He expressed support for the Palestinian-led boycott, divestment and sanctions movement, or BDS.
Organizers advocated for economic and cultural pressure on Israel to end the country’s occupation of territories captured in the 1967 Middle East war, grant full equality to Arab citizens of Israel and promote the rights of Palestinian refugees to return.
PEN America says it “emphatically opposes any efforts to inhibit the free international exchange of literature, art, information, or knowledge, including academic and cultural boycotts”. The group says it also defends the rights of individuals to “be protected from retaliatory efforts” for participating in boycotts.
Mengiste told the AP that PEN Writes takes a broader view, supporting boycotts themselves.
In July, in the aftermath of Mengestu’s departure, PEN America issued a statement citing such initiatives as its direction of $500,000 in emergency aid to Palestinians in Gaza, its legal support for a pro-Palestinian activist threatened with deportation by Donald Trump’s administration, and a 2025 PEN report entitled All That Is Lost: The Cultural Destruction of Gaza.
The new group is aiming for recognition at the PEN International Congress in Montenegro in September 2027. The process includes forming a steering committee, establishing communication with the PEN International secretariat and “seeking interest from the full diversity of writers” in a given country, according to PEN International’s guidelines.
Other prominent members of PEN Writes include Pulitzer prize winner Percival Everett, literary agent Nicole Aragi and novelist Hannah Lillith Assadi, who on Wednesday won the National Book Award for fiction.
Mengiste said PEN Writes aims to be effective as a more stripped-down, egalitarian organization run entirely by writers on behalf of writers.
“I think writers know first-hand what self-censorship or lost contracts or de-platforming looks like,” she told the AP. “We know that what comes for one writer will very likely come for others. We are guardians of each other as much as we are stewards of literature. We do not work with a writers organization, we ARE writers, organized and mobilized to defend all writers.”
The Associated Press contributed reporting
digest_he:
יותר ממאה סופרים ואנשי ספרות בארצות הברית הודיעו על הקמת שלוחה חדשה בשם PEN Writes US, כפיצול מארגון חופש הביטוי והזכויות הספרותיות PEN America. המהלך מגיע בעקבות מתיחות רבת-משקל סביב עמדות הארגון בנוגע למלחמה של ישראל בעזה וסוגיות נוספות.

המייסדים, הכוללים בין היתר את טה-ניהאסי קואטס, אם גסן וז'קלין וודסון, מבהירים כי הקבוצה החדשה לא נועדה להיות יריבה של PEN America, אלא להוות מסגרת שוויונית שתנוהל ישירות בידי סופרים ותפעל באופן עקבי להגנה על חופש הביטוי ונגד צנזורא.

הקרע בארגון הוחרף בעקבות ביקורת ציבורית על אופן התנהלותו של PEN America מאז אוקטובר 2023, שהובילה בעבר לביטול אירועים מרכזיים ולהתפטרותו של נשיא הארגון דינאו מנגסטו. הקבוצה החדשה שואפת לקבל הכרה רשמית מטעם PEN International בשנת 2027.
